stem: The branch of biology that studies the interactions of organisms with one another and their environment is __________.
solution: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their environment.

stem: The term 'ecology' was coined by __________.
solution: The term ecology was coined by Ernst Haeckel.

stem: The term 'ecosystem' was coined by __________.
solution: The term ecosystem was coined by A. G. Tansley.

stem: A functional unit of nature comprising living organisms and their non-living environment interacting together is a(n) __________.
solution: An ecosystem is the functional unit of biotic and abiotic components interacting.

stem: The two components of an ecosystem are biotic and __________.
solution: An ecosystem has biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components.

stem: Organisms that synthesise their own food are called __________.
solution: Producers (autotrophs), mainly green plants, make their own food.

stem: Organisms that break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients are __________.
solution: Decomposers (saprotrophs) break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.

stem: In a food chain, herbivores occupy the __________ trophic level.
solution: Herbivores (primary consumers) occupy the second trophic level; producers are the first.

stem: The interconnected network of many food chains in an ecosystem is called a __________.
solution: A food web is the network of interconnected food chains.

stem: A food chain that begins with dead organic matter is called a __________ food chain.
solution: The detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter (detritus).

stem: According to Lindeman's ten per cent law, the energy transferred to the next trophic level is about __________.
solution: About 10% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat.

stem: Energy flow in an ecosystem is __________.
solution: Energy flows in one direction through an ecosystem, unlike nutrients which cycle.

stem: The ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems is the __________.
solution: The Sun is the ultimate energy source for nearly all ecosystems.

stem: The total amount of organic matter produced by producers per unit area per unit time is the __________.
solution: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total organic matter produced by producers.

stem: Net primary productivity (NPP) equals GPP minus __________.
solution: NPP = GPP − respiration losses by producers; it is the biomass available to consumers.

stem: The graphical representation of trophic levels showing number, biomass or energy is an __________.
solution: Ecological pyramids depict trophic structure by number, biomass or energy.

stem: The ecological pyramid that is always upright (never inverted) is the pyramid of __________.
solution: The pyramid of energy is always upright because energy is lost at each level.

stem: The pyramid of biomass in an ocean (sea) ecosystem is usually __________.
solution: In oceans the biomass pyramid is inverted, as tiny phytoplankton support larger consumers.

stem: The pyramid of numbers in a single large tree ecosystem is typically __________.
solution: In a tree ecosystem the pyramid of numbers is inverted (one tree supports many insects/birds).

stem: The zone of transition between two ecosystems is called an __________.
solution: An ecotone is the transition zone between two ecosystems.

stem: The greater diversity of species found in the transition zone (ecotone) is called the __________ effect.
solution: The edge effect refers to the higher species diversity often found in ecotones.

stem: A species whose presence is essential for maintaining the structure of an ecological community is a __________ species.
solution: A keystone species has a disproportionately large role in maintaining community structure.

stem: The functional role and position of a species in its ecosystem is called its __________.
solution: The ecological niche is the functional role and position of a species in its ecosystem.

stem: The physical place where an organism lives is its __________.
solution: A habitat is the physical location where an organism lives.

stem: A large regional ecosystem characterised by a distinct climate and vegetation is a __________.
solution: A biome is a large-scale ecosystem defined by climate and dominant vegetation.

stem: The biome with the highest biodiversity on Earth is the __________.
solution: Tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity of all biomes.

stem: The cold, treeless biome found in the far north is the __________.
solution: The tundra is the cold, treeless biome of the far north (and high mountains).

stem: The coniferous forest biome, also called boreal forest, is the __________.
solution: The taiga (boreal forest) is the coniferous forest biome.

stem: The increase in concentration of a toxicant at successive trophic levels is called __________.
solution: Biomagnification is the increasing concentration of toxins up the food chain.

stem: The build-up of a toxic substance within the tissues of a single organism over time is called __________.
solution: Bioaccumulation is the accumulation of a toxin within one organism over its lifetime.

stem: A group of organisms of the same species living in a particular area is a __________.
solution: A population is a group of individuals of one species in an area.

stem: All the interacting populations of different species in an area form a __________.
solution: A biological community is all interacting populations in an area.

stem: The part of the Earth and its atmosphere where life exists is the __________.
solution: The biosphere is the global zone where life exists.

stem: The amount of living matter (biomass) present in an ecosystem at a given time is the __________.
solution: The standing crop is the total biomass present in an ecosystem at a given moment.

stem: Animals that feed on both plants and animals are called __________.
solution: Omnivores eat both plants and animals.

stem: Organisms like earthworms that feed on detritus (dead matter) are called __________.
solution: Detritivores such as earthworms feed on detritus.

stem: The vast majority of energy at each trophic level is lost as __________.
solution: Most energy at each level is lost as heat via respiration and metabolic activity.

stem: A species used to indicate the health or quality of an environment is a(n) __________ species.
solution: An indicator species reflects the condition of its environment (e.g. lichens for air quality).

stem: A charismatic species used to raise support for conservation is a __________ species.
solution: A flagship species (e.g. the tiger) is used to rally public support for conservation.

stem: Grazing food chains usually begin with __________.
solution: Grazing food chains start with living green plants (producers).

stem: The maximum number of trophic levels in a food chain is limited by __________.
options: the loss of energy at each level
solution: Energy loss (~90%) at each level limits food chains to usually 3–4 trophic levels.

stem: The productivity of consumers (their formation of new biomass) is called __________ productivity.
solution: Secondary productivity is the rate of biomass formation by consumers.

stem: In an ecosystem, nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen are __________.
solution: Nutrients cycle within the ecosystem, unlike energy which flows one way.

stem: The most productive natural ecosystems on Earth are __________.
solution: Tropical rainforests, coral reefs and estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems.

stem: A desert ecosystem is characterised by __________.
solution: Deserts have very low rainfall and sparse, drought-adapted vegetation.

stem: The pyramid of energy is expressed in units of __________.
options: energy per unit area per unit time
solution: The energy pyramid uses energy per unit area per unit time (e.g. kcal/m²/yr).

stem: The 'law of the minimum' (Liebig's law) states that growth is limited by the __________.
solution: Liebig's law of the minimum states that growth is limited by the scarcest essential nutrient/resource.

stem: The abiotic factors of an ecosystem include light, temperature, water and __________.
solution: Abiotic factors include light, temperature, water, soil and minerals.

stem: Primary consumers in a grassland ecosystem are typically __________.
solution: Primary consumers (herbivores) in a grassland include grasshoppers and grazing animals.

stem: An organism that occupies more than one trophic level in a food web is usually a(n) __________.
solution: Omnivores can occupy more than one trophic level as they eat plants and animals.

stem: The overall study of the structure and function of ecosystems is central to understanding __________.
solution: Ecosystem ecology explains how nature sustains life through energy flow and nutrient cycling.

stem: The 'trophic level' of an organism refers to its __________.
solution: A trophic level is an organism's feeding position in the food chain.

stem: The term 'ecology' was coined by the German biologist:
solution: Ernst Haeckel coined the term 'ecology' (Oekologie) in 1866, from the Greek 'oikos' (house) and 'logos' (study) — the study of organisms in relation to their environment.

stem: The term 'ecosystem' was coined by:
solution: A.G. Tansley coined 'ecosystem' in 1935, describing the integrated system of living organisms and their physical environment interacting as a unit.

stem: The most basic level of ecological organisation among the following is the:
solution: The hierarchy runs organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere. The individual organism is the most basic ecological level listed.

stem: A group of organisms of the same species living in a given area is a:
solution: A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species occupying a particular area at a given time.

stem: All the interacting populations of different species in an area form a:
solution: A biological community is the assemblage of all populations of different species living and interacting in a common area.

stem: The functional role and position of a species in its ecosystem (its 'profession') is called its:
solution: The ecological niche describes the functional role of a species — how it obtains food, its interactions and conditions it needs. The habitat is its 'address', the niche its 'profession'.

stem: The 'competitive exclusion principle' (Gause's principle) states that:
options: Two species can share an identical niche indefinitely
Two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely
solution: Gause's competitive exclusion principle holds that two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely; one will out-compete the other, or they must diverge (resource partitioning).

stem: Organisms that can tolerate a wide range of an environmental factor (e.g. temperature) are described as:
solution: The prefix 'eury' denotes a wide tolerance range (eurythermal = wide temperature tolerance; euryhaline = wide salinity tolerance). 'Steno' denotes a narrow range.

stem: Warm-blooded animals that maintain a constant body temperature are called:
solution: Homeotherms (endotherms) — birds and mammals — regulate a constant internal temperature metabolically. Poikilotherms (ectotherms) like reptiles vary with the environment.

stem: According to Allen's rule, mammals in colder climates tend to have:
options: Shorter ears and limbs to reduce heat loss
solution: Allen's rule states that endotherms in cold climates have shorter extremities (ears, limbs) to reduce surface area and conserve heat. Bergmann's rule adds that they tend to be larger-bodied.

stem: The dormancy that helps some animals survive cold winters by lowering metabolism is called:
solution: Hibernation is winter dormancy (e.g. bears, some rodents) to escape cold; aestivation is summer dormancy to escape heat and desiccation.

stem: Plants adapted to grow in dry, arid conditions are called:
solution: Xerophytes (e.g. cacti) are adapted to dry conditions with features like reduced leaves, thick cuticles and water storage. Hydrophytes live in water; halophytes in saline soils.

stem: The energy that enters almost all ecosystems ultimately comes from:
solution: Solar energy, captured by producers through photosynthesis, is the primary energy source for nearly all ecosystems (deep-sea chemosynthetic vents being a rare exception).

stem: Organisms that synthesise their own food using inorganic substances and light/chemical energy are:
solution: Autotrophs (producers) — green plants, algae, cyanobacteria — make their own organic food. Heterotrophs (consumers) depend on others for food.

stem: In an ecosystem, herbivores are classified as:
solution: Herbivores that feed directly on producers (plants) are primary consumers. Carnivores eating herbivores are secondary consumers, and so on.

stem: Organisms that feed on dead and decaying organic matter, breaking it down, are:
solution: Decomposers (saprotrophs) — bacteria and fungi — break down dead organic matter, recycling nutrients back to the soil and completing nutrient cycles.

stem: The role of decomposers in an ecosystem is chiefly to:
options: Recycle nutrients by breaking down dead organic matter
solution: Decomposers release nutrients locked in dead organisms back into the soil and atmosphere, making them available again to producers — essential for nutrient cycling.

stem: The 'standing crop' of a trophic level refers to the:
options: Amount of living biomass present at a given time
solution: Standing crop is the biomass (or number of individuals) present in a trophic level at any given time, usually expressed as mass of living matter per unit area.

stem: According to the '10 per cent law' of energy transfer (Lindeman), the energy passed to the next trophic level is about:
solution: Lindeman's 10% law states that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is lost mainly as heat in metabolism.

stem: Because of the 10% energy law, food chains rarely have more than:
solution: Since energy declines sharply at each level, little remains after 4–5 levels to support further consumers, so food chains are typically short.

stem: An ecological pyramid of energy is always:
solution: A pyramid of energy is always upright because usable energy decreases at each successive trophic level (10% law) and can never increase upward.

stem: The pyramid of numbers in a single large tree ecosystem (tree → birds → parasites) is:
solution: In a tree-based food chain, one tree supports many herbivorous birds, which support even more parasites, giving an inverted pyramid of numbers.

stem: A food web is more stable than a simple food chain because it:
options: Has only one path of energy flow
Provides alternative feeding pathways, buffering against species loss
solution: A food web's interconnected feeding relationships offer alternative energy routes, so the loss of one species is less likely to collapse the whole system — giving greater stability.

stem: The two basic types of food chains are the grazing food chain and the:
solution: The grazing food chain starts with living producers; the detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter (detritus) consumed by detritivores and decomposers.

stem: The gross primary productivity (GPP) minus respiration equals:
solution: NPP = GPP − respiration losses. NPP is the energy/biomass available to consumers (herbivores and decomposers) after producers meet their own metabolic needs.

stem: Which ecosystem has the highest net primary productivity per unit area?
solution: Tropical rainforests and coral reefs (and estuaries) have among the highest primary productivity, thanks to abundant light, warmth, water and nutrients. Deserts and open oceans are low.

stem: The 'edge effect' in ecology refers to the:
options: Greater diversity often found at the boundary (ecotone) between two ecosystems
solution: An ecotone is the transition zone between two communities; it often shows greater species richness and density (the edge effect), including some 'edge species' unique to it.

stem: Symbiotic relationship in which both interacting species benefit is:
solution: In mutualism both partners benefit (e.g. pollinators and flowering plants, mycorrhizae). Commensalism benefits one with no effect on the other; parasitism benefits one at the other's cost.

stem: The relationship between a cattle egret and grazing cattle (the egret feeds on insects flushed by the cattle) is an example of:
solution: This is commensalism — the egret benefits by catching disturbed insects, while the cattle are essentially unaffected.

stem: Lichens, a classic example of mutualism, are an association between a fungus and:
solution: A lichen is a mutualistic partnership: the fungus provides structure and protection, while the photosynthetic alga/cyanobacterium provides food. Lichens are also sensitive pollution indicators.

stem: Mycorrhizae represent a mutualism between fungi and:
solution: Mycorrhizae are mutualistic associations between fungi and plant roots; the fungus aids water/mineral (especially phosphorus) uptake while receiving sugars from the plant.

stem: An interaction where one species is harmed and the other is unaffected is:
solution: Amensalism harms one species while the other is unaffected — e.g. Penicillium releasing antibiotics that kill nearby bacteria without benefit or harm to itself.

stem: A biome is best defined as a:
options: Large regional ecosystem characterised by its dominant vegetation and climate
solution: A biome is a large geographic biotic unit — e.g. tropical rainforest, desert, tundra, grassland — defined by its climate and characteristic vegetation and animal life.

stem: The tundra biome is characterised by:
options: Permafrost, low temperatures and treeless vegetation
solution: The tundra (Arctic and alpine) has permanently frozen subsoil (permafrost), very cold temperatures, short growing seasons and low, treeless vegetation like mosses and lichens.

stem: The layer of Earth that supports all life — including parts of the land, water and air — is the:
solution: The biosphere is the global sum of all ecosystems — the zone of life encompassing parts of the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere where organisms exist.

stem: Abiotic components of an ecosystem include all EXCEPT:
solution: Abiotic (non-living) components are physical/chemical factors like light, temperature, water, air, soil and pH. Bacteria and fungi are biotic (living) components.

stem: 'Productivity' in an aquatic ecosystem is often limited by the availability of:
options: Light and nutrients (like nitrogen and phosphorus)
solution: Light penetration and nutrient (N, P) availability commonly limit aquatic primary productivity, which is why nutrient-rich upwelling zones and estuaries are highly productive.

stem: A 'keystone species' is defined by its:
options: Disproportionately large effect on community structure relative to its abundance
solution: A keystone species exerts an outsized influence on its ecosystem's structure and function relative to its numbers; its removal can cause dramatic changes (e.g. sea otters, tigers, figs).

stem: Nocturnal desert animals stay in burrows during the day mainly to:
options: Avoid extreme daytime heat and water loss
solution: Desert animals are often nocturnal or fossorial (burrowing) to avoid intense daytime heat and reduce water loss, emerging at night when it is cooler.

stem: The process by which lake ecosystems naturally age and fill in over long periods, becoming marshes and eventually land, is called:
solution: Over time, sediment and organic matter accumulate, nutrients enrich the water (natural eutrophication), and hydrarch succession converts a lake into marsh and eventually terrestrial community.

stem: Which of the following is a density-dependent factor regulating population size?
solution: Density-dependent factors (competition, predation, disease, food supply) intensify as population density rises. Density-independent factors (floods, fires, disasters) act regardless of density.

stem: An 'exponential' (J-shaped) growth curve of a population changes to a 'logistic' (S-shaped) curve because of:
options: Environmental resistance and carrying capacity limits
solution: As a population grows, limited resources and environmental resistance slow growth, producing an S-shaped logistic curve that levels off at the carrying capacity (K).

stem: The maximum population size an environment can sustainably support is its:
solution: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum number of individuals of a species that an environment can support indefinitely given its resources.

stem: Trophic level of an organism refers to its:
options: Position in the food chain based on feeding relationship
solution: A trophic level indicates an organism's feeding position — producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, etc. — in the food chain.

stem: In deep-sea hydrothermal vent ecosystems, the primary producers obtain energy through:
solution: Without sunlight, deep-sea vent producers are chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidise inorganic chemicals (e.g. H2S) to make food — one of the rare non-solar-based ecosystems.

stem: 'Bioaccumulation' differs from 'biomagnification' in that bioaccumulation refers to the build-up of a pollutant:
options: Within a single organism over its lifetime
solution: Bioaccumulation is the gradual build-up of a substance within one organism over time; biomagnification is the increase in concentration up successive trophic levels of a food chain.

stem: The two ecosystems generally regarded as the most productive on Earth are:
options: Estuaries and coral reefs (with tropical rainforests on land)
solution: Estuaries, coral reefs, tropical rainforests and swamps/marshes rank as the most productive ecosystems, while open oceans, deserts and tundra are among the least productive per unit area.

stem: Which statement about the flow of energy and nutrients in an ecosystem is correct?
options: Both energy and nutrients are recycled
Energy flows one way (and is lost as heat) while nutrients are recycled
Nutrients flow one way, energy is recycled
solution: Energy flow is unidirectional — entering as sunlight and dissipating as heat, so it must be continuously supplied. Nutrients, by contrast, are cycled repeatedly through biogeochemical cycles.
